forward-stride-simulation-with-band.name: Forward Stride Simulation with Band
forward-stride-simulation-with-band.execution: Anchor a band low behind you. Loop it around one ankle. Stand in an athletic position, banded leg slightly behind. Drive the banded leg back and down — full hip extension against the band resistance. Hold the extended position 1 second — squeeze the glute fully. Return to start under control. The band pulls you back through the return. Complete all reps one leg, then switch. Focus on the push-off mechanic.
forward-stride-simulation-with-band.why: The band-resisted forward stride simulation replicates the exact hip extension and push-off mechanics of a skating stride while standing — allowing players to groove the neuromuscular pattern daily without ice access. By adding band resistance behind the driving leg, it overloads the glutes and hip extensors in the exact position of peak force production in the skating stride.
forward-stride-simulation-with-band.transfer: Resisted forward stride — builds skating push-off against resistance. Pair with slide board work for full skating-pattern coverage. Forward extension + lateral push = complete stride.
forward-stride-simulation-with-band.cues: "Band anchored behind" · "Exaggerate stride extension" · "Full hip extension each step"
forward-stride-simulation-with-band.mistakes: Rotating the hip instead of extending it — drive back, not sideways. Not achieving full hip extension — the glute must fire at end-range. Arching the lower back to fake more extension — posterior pelvic tilt and squeeze. Moving too fast — this is a motor pattern drill. Slow and deliberate beats fast and sloppy.
forward-stride-simulation-with-band.progression: Progress: Add a simultaneous arm drive opposite to the leg — full skating stride simulation. | Regress: Bodyweight hip extension (donkey kick) — same pattern with zero resistance.

lateral-crossover-step-up.name: Lateral Crossover Step-Up
lateral-crossover-step-up.execution: Stand sideways to a box (40-50cm high). The far foot will lead. Cross the far foot OVER and UP onto the box — the crossover step. Drive through the box foot to stand fully on top of the box. Step down with the same crossing pattern on the other side. Or: step back down the same side and repeat the crossover for all reps before switching. Add dumbbells as bodyweight becomes easy.
lateral-crossover-step-up.why: The lateral crossover step-up combines a crossover foot pattern with a vertical step-up — training the hip abductors, adductors, and glutes in the exact lateral-then-vertical force direction of a crossover stride. This is one of the most hockey-specific strength exercises available for forwards and defensemen who rely on explosive crossovers to generate speed through turns.
lateral-crossover-step-up.transfer: Single-leg crossover power — builds edge-to-edge power for tight turns. Pair with skater jumps for full lateral coverage. Strength + plyo for the same pattern.
lateral-crossover-step-up.cues: "Stand beside box" · "Step up crossover with lead leg" · "Drive up" · "Step down other side"
lateral-crossover-step-up.mistakes: Pushing off the floor foot — all drive must come from the box foot. Box too low — below knee height doesn't create enough demand. No crossover — a straight step-up misses the lateral hip loading entirely. Fast and sloppy — control the movement. The crossover mechanics matter.',.
lateral-crossover-step-up.progression: Progress: Add a lateral jump at the top of the step-up — explosive single-leg lateral power.', | Regress: Standard step-up — master unilateral vertical drive before adding the crossover pattern.',

mini-band-lateral-walk.name: Mini-Band Lateral Walk
mini-band-lateral-walk.execution: Place a mini-band just above the knees or around the ankles (harder).',. Stand in an athletic stance — knees slightly bent, hips loaded.',. Step laterally with the lead foot, then follow with the trail foot.',. Maintain constant tension on the band — feet never come together.',. Take 10-15 steps in one direction, then 10-15 back.',. Keep the torso upright — do not lean side to side.',.
mini-band-lateral-walk.why: The mini-band lateral walk is the most accessible glute med activation exercise available — no equipment needed beyond a $5 band. It builds the hip abductor endurance that stabilises the pelvis across an entire game's worth of skating strides. Research shows that 6 weeks of mini-band lateral walk training significantly reduces hip drop during single-leg tasks — directly translating to more powerful and efficient skating strides.
mini-band-lateral-walk.transfer: Activates the glute medius — critical for lateral push and stability in skating. Daily activation drill, especially before skating or squatting. Free fix for chronic crossover weakness.
mini-band-lateral-walk.cues: "Band above knees" · "Stay low in athletic stance" · "Step wide" · "Keep tension in band"
mini-band-lateral-walk.mistakes: Feet coming together — kills the tension. Always keep the band taut.',. Torso swaying — the movement is entirely in the hips. Torso stays quiet.',. Band around the knees when you're ready for ankles — ankles creates longer lever, more demand.',. Too wide steps — quality steps with constant tension beats wide sloppy ones.',.
mini-band-lateral-walk.progression: Progress: Monster walk (band at ankles, forward diagonal steps) — adds hip flexor and abductor demand.', | Regress: Band above the knees with very light resistance — easiest starting point.',

mirror-drill.name: Mirror Drill
mirror-drill.execution: Face a partner 2 meters apart. Both in athletic stance — low, on the balls of the feet. Partner moves side-to-side randomly. Your job: MIRROR them — same direction, same speed. Stay low. Don't cross your feet. Shuffle. 20-30 second rounds. Switch leader. Repeat. Progress: add forward/back movement. Add a ball drop or visual cue (raised hand) for direction change. Solo version: react to a phone-app cue (a Tabata timer with random beeps) or coin flip every 2 seconds.
mirror-drill.why: Mirror drill trains REACTIVE agility — the cognitive-to-motor speed of responding to an unpredictable opponent. Where pre-planned agility drills (cone weaves, ladder patterns) train movement quality, mirror drills train the DECISION-and-execute pipeline that wins 1-on-1 battles. Reactive agility scores predict actual game performance far better than planned agility tests. For hockey players, this is the closest off-ice analogue to gap control on a defender or angling the puck carrier — you can't plan the route; you have to read and react.
mirror-drill.transfer: Reactive footwork — the EXACT skill of defending in 1-on-1 situations. You can't pre-plan it; you have to react. Trains the brain-to-feet path that separates great defenders from average ones. Defenders: this is your daily homework. Forwards: this is what beats defenders. Train both sides.
mirror-drill.cues: "Face a partner (or imaginary opponent) about 2m apart. They move side to side" · "Randomly. Your job: MIRROR them. Same direction" · "Same speed. Stay low" · "On the balls of your feet. Switch leader every 20-30 sec. Solo version: react to a coin flip or a phone timer beep."
mirror-drill.mistakes: Standing tall between reactions — defeats the purpose. Stay LOW and ready. Anticipating the partner's next move — they should be unpredictable. If they're predictable, the drill is broken. Crossing feet during the shuffle — slows the reverse direction. Always step then close, never cross. Doing too long rounds — quality dies past 30 seconds. Short rounds, full intent.
mirror-drill.progression: Progress: 3D mirror — forward/back/lateral cues; tests omnidirectional reactivity. | Regress: Slow mirror — leader moves at 50% speed; lets the follower catch the pattern before adding speed.

reaction-ball-drop.name: Reaction Ball Drop
reaction-ball-drop.execution: Hold the ball at chest height with one hand. Drop it. Let it bounce ONCE on the floor. React to the irregular bounce and catch it before the second bounce. Switch hands. Repeat. Progress 1: drop with one hand, catch with the other. Progress 2: drop, clap your hands, then catch. Progress 3: drop, turn 180°, catch.
reaction-ball-drop.why: Reaction speed separates a turnover from a steal — and the reaction ball drop trains it specifically by introducing IRREGULAR, UNPREDICTABLE bouncing patterns. Where a tennis ball bounces predictably, a reaction ball (with its lumpy 6-sided shape) bounces randomly, forcing the brain to track + decide + execute in milliseconds. This is the closest off-ice analogue to reading a deflected puck, an erratic pass, or a tipped shot. Six to eight weeks of irregular-cue training reduces reaction times by 10-15%.
reaction-ball-drop.transfer: Reaction speed is what separates a turnover from a steal. Trains the brain-to-hand pathway under irregular, unpredictable conditions — exactly what hockey demands. Hockey is a reaction sport disguised as a strategic one. Train the reflex daily.
reaction-ball-drop.cues: "Hold a tennis or reaction ball at chest height. Drop it. Catch it after ONE bounce — but the bounce is random. Add layers: drop with one hand" · "Catch with the other. Drop" · "Clap" · "Catch."
reaction-ball-drop.mistakes: Anticipating the bounce — defeats the purpose. The brain must react, not predict. Using a tennis ball as a substitute — too predictable; you need the irregular surface. Looking away during the drop — your visual tracking IS the training target. Catching with both hands every time — train one-handed catches both sides.
reaction-ball-drop.progression: Progress: Add a cognitive task — count backwards from 100 by 7s while reacting. Tests dual-task processing. | Regress: Tennis ball drop — same protocol, predictable bounce. Builds catching mechanics before adding randomness.
reaction-ball-drop.muscles: Reaction time, Hand-eye coordination, Cognitive processing

resisted-lateral-shuffle.name: Resisted Lateral Shuffle
resisted-lateral-shuffle.execution: Place a resistance band around both ankles or have a partner hold a band at your hips. Assume a hockey stance — knees bent, hips loaded, slight forward lean. Shuffle laterally against the resistance, maintaining constant hip width. Stay low — do not let the hips rise as you shuffle. Drive the lead foot out and follow with the trail foot — never let feet cross. 10-15 shuffles each direction, rest, repeat.
resisted-lateral-shuffle.why: The band-resisted lateral shuffle overloads the hip abductors and adductors during lateral movement — the exact muscles that drive crossovers and defensive gap-control slides. By adding resistance to a movement pattern the athlete already knows, it builds sport-specific lateral strength without changing the mechanics. Players who do resisted lateral shuffles consistently show measurable improvements in lateral skating speed within 4-6 weeks.
resisted-lateral-shuffle.transfer: Builds lateral power under resistance — stronger crossovers and edge work. Useful for defensemen and goalies especially. The pattern is what an angled-skate push feels like under load.
resisted-lateral-shuffle.cues: "Band at waist" · "Partner resists laterally" · "Drive hard to each side" · "Stay low"
resisted-lateral-shuffle.mistakes: Feet crossing — this becomes a crossover, not a shuffle. Keep feet apart. Standing tall to reduce the effort — the crouch is mandatory. Short, choppy steps — drive the lead foot out aggressively. Only going one direction — both directions equally important.
resisted-lateral-shuffle.progression: Progress: Resisted crossover shuffle — add the crossover foot pattern against resistance. | Regress: Mini-band lateral walk — same muscles, less speed demand.

slide-board-crossover-simulation.name: Slide Board — Crossover Simulation
slide-board-crossover-simulation.execution: Set the slide board on a flat surface. Wear booties or smooth socks. Stand on one end in an athletic stance — knees slightly bent, hips loaded. Cross-step the LEAD foot over the other, planting on the far edge. Push HARD off the back foot's outside edge — same as a crossover. Glide across the board, keeping low, weight over mid-foot. Plant on the far side, decelerate, and reverse direction. Build to 30-45 seconds continuous for conditioning, or 6-8 reps each side for power.
slide-board-crossover-simulation.why: The slide board crossover is the closest off-ice movement to actual skating — it trains the exact lateral push pattern of a crossover with proper edge mechanics. NHL development programs use this 3-4×/week in season because it maintains skating-specific neuromuscular patterns when ice time is limited. Reduces atrophy of the adductors/abductors that stride muscles.
slide-board-crossover-simulation.transfer: Directly trains the crossover pattern — improves cornering speed. Skating fluidity translates from this drill faster than from any other off-ice exercise. Earned by repetition.
slide-board-crossover-simulation.cues: "Cross lead foot over" · "Push off outside edge" · "Drive across board" · "Repeat"
slide-board-crossover-simulation.mistakes: Standing too tall — kills the edge engagement. Stay low like in your hockey stance. Pushing off the wrong edge — the OUTSIDE edge of the back skate is what propels you. Same here. Not crossing the foot fully over — short steps don't simulate a real crossover. Going too fast for form — slow down, get the mechanics right, then add speed.
slide-board-crossover-simulation.progression: Progress: Add a band around hips for resistance, OR use a longer slide board (8'+) for more force absorption demand. | Regress: Lateral mini-band walks first — builds glute med endurance before adding the slide board impact.

slide-board-lateral-stride.name: Slide Board — Lateral Stride
slide-board-lateral-stride.execution: Place slide board on flat surface. Wear booties or smooth socks. Stand at one end in a hockey stance — knees bent, hips loaded. Push off the outside edge of one foot, extending the hip and knee fully. Glide to the other end. Absorb with the landing leg. Push off again immediately — continuous rhythmic strides. Stay low throughout — stand up and you lose the skating-specific benefit.
slide-board-lateral-stride.why: The slide board stride simulates the lateral push mechanics of skating more closely than any other off-ice exercise — the glide, push, and weight transfer are nearly identical to skating with edges. It trains the hip abductors and adductors under skating-specific loading while keeping the movement pattern neurally familiar. NHL teams use slide boards daily in-season to maintain skating-specific neuromuscular patterns between games.
slide-board-lateral-stride.transfer: The closest off-ice skating simulation — trains exact stride mechanics. Goalies double the dose. Slide board is your lateral push-off drill. Direct transfer.
slide-board-lateral-stride.cues: "Push hard off bumper" · "Reach full extension" · "Glide" · "Recover" · "Push again"
slide-board-lateral-stride.mistakes: Standing tall — you must stay in the hockey crouch the entire time. Short pushes — full hip and knee extension on every stride. Looking down — eyes forward, same as on the ice. Going too fast for form — controlled mechanics beat sloppy speed.
slide-board-lateral-stride.progression: Progress: Add a resistance band at the hips for external loading against the stride. | Regress: Mini-band lateral walk — same muscles, stationary, lower demand entry point.

stickhandling-tennis-ball.name: Stickhandling — Tennis Ball
stickhandling-tennis-ball.execution: Hockey stick + tennis ball on a flat, smooth surface (garage floor, driveway). Soft hands — the stick blade cushions the ball like an extension of your fingers. Start with front-to-back stickhandling — controlled, deliberate. 30 seconds. Then side-to-side — heel-to-toe of the blade. 30 seconds. Figure-8 around feet, toe-drag pull, between-the-legs. Build the catalog. EYES UP — feel the ball, don't stare at it. This is the hardest and most important part.
stickhandling-tennis-ball.why: A tennis ball is HARDER to control with a hockey stick than a puck — it's lighter, bouncier, has higher center of gravity, and demands softer hands. Master a tennis ball and the puck feels glued to your blade. Wayne Gretzky famously did this drill every day as a kid in his backyard; modern pros from Patrick Kane to Auston Matthews still build their off-ice stickhandling on a tennis ball foundation. The fine-motor skill acquired here is the literal definition of hockey hands — the soft-hand control that creates time and space on the ice.
stickhandling-tennis-ball.transfer: A tennis ball is harder to control than a puck — slower, bouncier, requires lighter touch. Master a tennis ball and the puck feels easy. Wayne Gretzky famously did this every day as a kid. Master the tennis ball and the puck feels glued to your blade. Soft hands compound over years.
stickhandling-tennis-ball.cues: "Hockey stick + tennis ball on a flat surface. Soft hands — let the stick blade cushion the ball. Front-to-back. Side-to-side. Figure-8. Toe-drag pull. Eyes UP — feel the ball" · "Don't stare at it."
stickhandling-tennis-ball.mistakes: Staring at the ball — defeats the actual game skill. Eyes up forces feel. Gripping the stick too tight — soft hands need a relaxed grip. Using too small a surface area — work in a 6×6 ft zone minimum to allow real range. Skipping the weak side — every player has a worse hand. Spend MORE time there.
stickhandling-tennis-ball.progression: Progress: Golf ball stickhandling — smaller, harder to track. Pros use this as the elite progression. | Regress: Stickhandling with a regular puck on slick floor — same patterns, easier object control.

stride-lunge-with-reach.name: Stride Lunge with Reach
stride-lunge-with-reach.execution: Stand tall. Step forward into a long lunge with the right foot. As you lower into the lunge, reach the LEFT arm forward and down toward the right foot. The right arm drives back — cross-body opposition, like a skating arm swing. Hold the bottom position 2 seconds — feel the hip flexor stretch of the rear leg. Drive through the front foot to return. Switch legs. Alternate continuously for 8-10 reps each side.
stride-lunge-with-reach.why: The stride lunge with reach combines the single-leg strength of a lunge with a contralateral arm reach — mimicking the rotational mechanics of a full skating stride where the opposite arm drives forward as the leg pushes back. This integrated pattern trains the cross-body coordination that separates efficient, fluid skaters from mechanical ones. It also develops significant hip flexor and thoracic mobility simultaneously.
stride-lunge-with-reach.transfer: Dynamic stretch that mimics the full skating stride extension. Useful as dynamic warm-up before skating or lower-body lifting. Two birds, one drill.
stride-lunge-with-reach.cues: "Lunge forward" · "Reach front arm forward and low (puck position)" · "Hold 2s" · "Alternate"
stride-lunge-with-reach.mistakes: No rotation — the reach must be cross-body and involve thoracic rotation. Short stride — take a genuinely long step to get the hip flexor stretch. Front knee caving inward — drive it out over the toes. Rushing through it — slow down to feel the rotational coordination.
stride-lunge-with-reach.progression: Progress: Add a light dumbbell in the reaching hand — increases rotational demand. | Regress: Standard forward lunge without the reach — master the lunge first.

tight-turn-simulation.name: Tight Turn Simulation
tight-turn-simulation.execution: Place a cone on the floor. Start 5m away. Sprint toward the cone at full speed. As you approach, lean the body INTO the turn — inside shoulder drops. Plant the outside foot and drive around the cone as tightly as possible. Accelerate hard out of the turn for 5-10m. Alternate direction of turn each rep.
tight-turn-simulation.why: Hockey tight turns are among the most technically demanding skating skills — requiring maximum edge pressure, hip rotation, and centripetal force absorption while maintaining top speed. Off-ice cone drill tight turns simulate the body lean, weight shift, and deceleration-reacceleration pattern that on-ice tight turns demand. Regular tight turn simulation measurably improves on-ice turn speed by reinforcing the lean-and-drive mechanics in the nervous system.
tight-turn-simulation.transfer: Mimics the tight turn in corners — essential for puck battles below the dots. Practice both directions. Most players have a strong-side turn and a weak-side turn — work the weak one harder.
tight-turn-simulation.cues: "Sprint to cone" · "Plant outside foot" · "Lean into turn" · "Come out of it accelerating"
tight-turn-simulation.mistakes: Wide arc around the cone — attack it. The tighter the arc, the better the transfer. Standing upright through the turn — lean into it. Low centre of gravity = faster turn. Not accelerating out of the turn — the exit acceleration is as important as the turn itself. Only turning one direction — always alternate left and right.
tight-turn-simulation.progression: Progress: Add a second cone (S-turn) — string two tight turns together with an acceleration between. | Regress: Walk the turn at 50% speed — internalise the lean mechanics before adding speed.

w-cone-drill.name: W-Cone Drill
w-cone-drill.execution: Set 5 cones in a W shape: one at each outer point and one at the center top. Sprint to the first outer cone, plant hard on the outside foot, cut back toward center. Continue through all 5 cones maintaining sprint-decelerate-cut rhythm. Drive through each cut with a low center of gravity — don't stand tall. Arms drive hard opposite to the cutting direction. Time the run. Full recovery between reps.
w-cone-drill.why: The W-drill trains multi-directional cutting ability — the capacity to accelerate, plant, and redirect at angles that mirror tight-turn edge work. Unlike the T-drill which is linear and lateral, the W-drill demands diagonal cutting which maps directly to angling opponents, driving wide around a defender, and cutting back to the middle off the wing.
w-cone-drill.transfer: Multi-directional change of direction — simulates open-ice skating patterns. Cone drills are pattern practice, not conditioning. Treat them with quality focus, not volume focus.
w-cone-drill.cues: "Sprint to each cone in W pattern" · "Sharp cuts" · "Stay low in turns"
w-cone-drill.mistakes: Wide, looping turns instead of sharp cuts — the plant-and-go must be aggressive. Standing tall through the cuts — low hips = faster direction change. Consistent weak-side bias — always run it both directions equally. Too many reps before full recovery — quality over quantity for agility training.
w-cone-drill.progression: Progress: Add a ball or puck-handling element at each cone — game-realistic dual-task demand. | Regress: Walk the pattern, then jog, then 75% before going full speed.

wall-ball-toss.name: Wall Ball Toss
wall-ball-toss.execution: Stand 2 m from a flat wall, tennis ball in one hand. Throw at the wall, catch with the SAME hand. 30 seconds per hand. Switch hands. Repeat. Progress 1: throw with right, catch with left. Switch. Progress 2: juggle two balls against the wall. Progress 3: one hand tosses, opposite hand catches — switch direction every 5 throws.
wall-ball-toss.why: Hand-eye coordination is the #1 trainable skill for puck reception, passing accuracy, and reaction time on the ice — and wall ball toss is the cheapest, most efficient way to train it. Five minutes of daily hand-eye work over 8 weeks produces measurable improvements in reaction time and visual tracking — the EXACT skills that turn an average puck handler into a great one. Pro players including Crosby and Kane have all gone on record citing daily ball-toss work as a foundational habit.
wall-ball-toss.transfer: Hand-eye coordination is the #1 trainable skill for puck reception, passing accuracy, and reaction time on the ice. Pros do this daily. Many pros cite ball-toss work as a foundational daily habit. The skill ceiling is built daily, not occasionally.
wall-ball-toss.cues: "Tennis ball + flat wall" · "2m away. Throw at the wall" · "Catch with the SAME hand. Switch hands. Progress: opposite hand catch" · "Juggle two balls" · "One hand toss / other hand catch. Goal — never drop it."
wall-ball-toss.mistakes: Throwing too hard — you'll drop more than you catch; this is precision work, not power. Standing too close (under 1.5 m) — gives no reaction time. Stand further to make it harder. Looking away from the ball — eye tracking is the actual training target. Skipping the weaker hand — every player has a 'non-stick hand' that drops more. Train it.
wall-ball-toss.progression: Progress: Two-ball juggle against the wall — concurrent visual tracking of two objects. | Regress: Ball drop — drop ball, catch after one bounce. Easier predictability, builds the catching reflex.
wall-ball-toss.muscles: Hand-eye coordination, Reaction time, Wrists, Forearms

crab-walk.name: Crab Walk
crab-walk.execution: Sit on the floor with feet flat, knees bent, hands flat behind you (fingers pointing toward your hips, NOT away). Lift the hips UP off the floor until the torso is roughly parallel to the ground. Walk forward (or backward, or sideways) by moving opposite hand and opposite foot together. Hips stay HIGH the entire time — never let them drop back down. Distance: 10-15 meters per trip. 3-4 trips total. Slow and controlled. Quality over speed.
crab-walk.why: The crab walk is the POSTERIOR mirror of the bear crawl — same contralateral coordination training, but loading the triceps, glutes, and posterior chain instead of the chest and quads. Critical for youth athletes because they spend so much time in flexion-dominant positions (sitting at desks, leaning forward to skate) that they lose the ability to extend the hips while bracing the shoulders. Crab walks reverse this: hips up, shoulders open, posterior chain firing.
crab-walk.transfer: Builds posterior-chain coordination + shoulder/triceps strength + core stability all at once. The opposite-pattern of bear crawl — kids love it, and it patterns the cross-body coordination hockey demands. Pair with bear crawl for full coordination day. Both contralateral patterns, both critical at 9-13.
crab-walk.cues: "Sit on the floor" · "Hands behind you flat on ground" · "Feet flat in front. Lift hips UP off the floor. Walk forward / backward / sideways" · "Moving opposite hand and foot. Hips stay HIGH the whole time."
crab-walk.mistakes: Hips dropping — turns it into a seated shuffle. Keep them lifted. Fingers pointing away from the body — torques the wrists and shoulders; reverse them. Moving same-side hand and foot — wrong pattern; must be opposite. Going too fast and losing form — pattern integrity matters more than distance covered.
crab-walk.progression: Progress: Crab walk with a band around the ankles — adds glute med activation. | Regress: Glute bridge hold (hips up, hold still, no walk) — builds the position before adding the walk.

cable-chop.name: Cable Chop
cable-chop.execution: Set a cable at shoulder height. Stand sideways to the machine. Grip the handle with both hands, arms extended. Feet shoulder-width. Brace the core hard. Begin with hips and shoulders facing the machine. Rotate away from the machine in one smooth arc — hips drive first, shoulders follow. Let the arms follow the torso rotation — don't pull with the arms alone. Control the return slowly — 3-second eccentric back to start.
cable-chop.why: The cable chop trains the rotational force transfer pattern that generates shot power and board battle leverage. It loads the core in a diagonal plane — exactly how rotational force travels from the ice through your body to the stick. Diagonal core loading builds the 'stiffness' that lets you transfer power without leaking energy through the spine.
cable-chop.transfer: Loaded diagonal chopping — exactly the power pattern of a slapshot. Cable chop trains rotational power with constant tension throughout the rep. No drop-off, no cheating.
cable-chop.cues: "Rotate from hips" · "Arms relatively straight" · "Follow through" · "Return with control"
cable-chop.mistakes: Pulling with the arms only — the power comes from hip rotation, not the arms. Letting the lower back rotate instead of the hips — keep the lumbar spine neutral. Too much weight — heavy loads slow the pattern and train grinding, not rotational speed. Skipping the eccentric — the slow return builds as much core strength as the chop.
cable-chop.progression: Progress: Half-kneeling cable chop — removes the legs, isolates the rotational core challenge. | Regress: Band pull-across — same rotation pattern with lower load and more stability.

cable-woodchop-explosive.name: Cable Woodchop (Explosive)
cable-woodchop-explosive.execution: Set the cable HIGH (shoulder height or above). Stand sideways, feet wide. Grip the handle with both hands. Load the hips toward the machine. Explosively rotate AWAY from the machine — drive the back hip through first. Arms follow the rotation in a downward diagonal arc — hips lead, shoulders follow, arms last. End in a low diagonal position, weight on the front foot. Reset slowly (3 seconds) back to start. Explosion is ONLY on the way down.
cable-woodchop-explosive.why: The explosive cable woodchop trains the high-velocity rotational power that produces slap shot speed. Unlike slow cable chops, the explosive version forces the nervous system to recruit fast-twitch muscle fibers in the rotational chain. Shot velocity studies show the fastest shooters in the NHL produce trunk rotation speeds exceeding 700°/second — training this system explosively is the direct path there.
cable-woodchop-explosive.transfer: Trains the high-to-low rotational chain used in slap shots. Cable provides constant tension through full ROM. Pair with med ball rotational throws for full rotational-power coverage. Cable adds constant tension; med ball adds release.
cable-woodchop-explosive.cues: "Cable set high" · "Rotate diagonally down explosively. Drive with hips first" · "Arms follow. Control return."
cable-woodchop-explosive.mistakes: Using arms to pull instead of hips to rotate — arms are just connectors, hips produce force. Going heavy — this must be FAST. Drop weight until the movement is explosive. Stopping at the end instead of decelerating through it — follow through like a slap shot. Equal speed both ways — slow reset, explosive chop. Not a reciprocal movement.
cable-woodchop-explosive.progression: Progress: Add a shuffle step into the chop (one lateral step before the rotation) — adds momentum like a real slapshot wind-up. | Regress: Slow cable chop — master the rotation pattern at controlled speed before going explosive.

landmine-rotation.name: Landmine Rotation
landmine-rotation.execution: Anchor a barbell in a landmine base or wedge it in a corner with weight on the far end. Stand facing the anchor, feet shoulder-width. Hold the weighted end with both hands. Begin with the bar at hip height on one side. Rotate the bar in an arc across the body — hips drive first, torso follows, arms last. Finish with the bar at hip height on the opposite side. Return under control. Equal reps each direction.
landmine-rotation.why: The landmine rotation trains rotational core strength in a safe, guided arc — the bar's fixed endpoint at the floor means it can't go out of plane, making it ideal for loading rotational power progressively. For hockey players it builds the core rotational strength that generates slap shot power and resists the torsional forces of taking a body check. The diagonal arc of the bar matches the actual direction of force in a wrist shot.
landmine-rotation.transfer: Loaded rotational power — the closest off-ice simulation of a wrist shot. Landmines are the gateway to rotational power without the spine cost of free-weight rotation work. Use them.
landmine-rotation.cues: "Hold end of bar at chest" · "Rotate to each side with hip drive" · "Stay athletic"
landmine-rotation.mistakes: Rotating with the arms only — hips must initiate. Arm-only rotation produces no power. Too much weight — heavy loads kill the arc speed. Moderate weight, high velocity. Upright posture — athletic stance with slight knee bend throughout. Ignoring the eccentric — slow controlled return builds as much strength as the rotation.
landmine-rotation.progression: Progress: Half-kneeling landmine rotation — removes the leg drive, isolates rotational core demand. | Regress: Cable chop at light weight — guided rotation with less load complexity.',

landmine-rotational-press.name: Landmine Rotational Press
landmine-rotational-press.execution: Load a landmine. Stand sideways to the anchor, bar held at shoulder height in both hands. Load the hips away from the anchor — this is the backswing. Drive the hips toward the anchor explosively, rotating the torso. As the torso rotates, press the bar upward and away — arms extend fully. The finish position: hips facing the anchor, arms extended above and across the body. Return under control. Complete all reps one side before switching.
landmine-rotational-press.why: The landmine rotational press combines hip rotation with an overhead press in a single explosive movement — training the full kinetic chain of a slap shot from the ground through the hands. It develops the linking strength between the lower body and upper body that defines elite shot power. Unlike isolated exercises, this movement forces the entire body to coordinate in a single explosive rotational arc.
landmine-rotational-press.transfer: Loaded rotational pressing — combines core rotation and upper body push, identical to the kinetic chain of a slap shot. Pair with med ball rotational throw. Both train the same chain; landmine adds load, med ball adds release velocity.
landmine-rotational-press.cues: "Barbell in landmine. Hold end at shoulder" · "Rotate through hips and press across body. BOTH sides equally."
landmine-rotational-press.mistakes: Pressing before rotating — the press is driven by the rotation, not independent of it. Using the arms to initiate — the sequence is feet → hips → torso → arms. Always. Bar too heavy — speed and coordination are the training stimuli, not maximum load. Neglecting the non-dominant side — shooting side and opposite side both matter.
landmine-rotational-press.progression: Progress: Single-arm landmine press with rotation — higher core demand and instability. | Regress: Landmine rotation without the press — master the hip drive before adding the press.',

med-ball-scoop-throw.name: Med Ball Scoop Throw
med-ball-scoop-throw.execution: Hold a med ball (4-6kg) between the legs. Stand athletic, knees bent.',. Load the hips back — slight hinge, ball hanging between knees. Explosively drive the hips forward — stand up fast and throw the ball UPWARD as high as possible. Release the ball at approximately waist height — let the hip drive send it skyward. Catch it (or let it bounce) and immediately reset for the next rep. Every rep maximum height — height is the measure of power output.',.
med-ball-scoop-throw.why: The med ball scoop throw trains the upward hip extension power that drives the skating push-off and the body-checking lift — the same triple extension pattern as an Olympic lift but with a medicine ball. The underhand scoop throw is one of the few exercises that trains concentric power production at maximum velocity with no deceleration phase (the ball just flies), making it highly effective at developing fast-twitch output.
med-ball-scoop-throw.transfer: Direct shooting transfer — same kinetic chain as a wrist shot or slap shot. Hip drive → core rotation → release. Pair with squat jumps for full lower-body power day. Loaded + unloaded, both directions.
med-ball-scoop-throw.cues: "Athletic stance" · "Ball at hip. Rotate through hips and core" · "Scoop the ball overhead and forward at a wall. Catch and reset."
med-ball-scoop-throw.mistakes: Using the arms to throw instead of the hips — the arms guide the ball, hips launch it. Ball too heavy — power output drops. 4-6kg is optimal for most.',. Not fully extending at the top — rise onto the toes, full triple extension.',. Slow tempo between reps — these should feel explosive and rhythmic.',.
med-ball-scoop-throw.progression: Progress: Single-leg scoop throw — adds unilateral skating-specific demand.', | Regress: Kettlebell swing — same hip drive pattern with less coordination demand.',

med-ball-shot-simulation.name: Med Ball Shot Simulation
med-ball-shot-simulation.execution: Hold a light med ball (2-3kg) in a shooting grip — dominant hand forward. Stand in your shooting stance — weight on the back foot.',. Rotate the hips and shift weight to the front foot — exactly like a wrist shot load.',. Release the ball against a rebounder or wall in a wrist shot motion.',. Follow through fully — dominant hand finishes high, same as a real shot.',. 10-15 rapid fire reps, then switch to backhand simulation.',.
med-ball-shot-simulation.why: The med ball shot simulation replicates the rotational mechanics of a wrist shot or snapshot at high velocity — training the exact kinetic chain sequence of stick-to-puck power transfer. By using a heavier object (2-4kg) than a puck, it builds the rotational strength that makes the actual shot feel lighter and faster. Repeated at high reps it also builds the rotational endurance for sustained shot power late in shifts.
med-ball-shot-simulation.transfer: The closest off-ice movement to an actual hockey shot. Same hip rotation, same weight transfer, same release mechanics. Useful pre-season or off-season to drill shot mechanics under load. Skip in-season — too much volume for the same pattern.
med-ball-shot-simulation.cues: "Stand in shooting stance. Load weight back foot" · "Drive forward through hips" · "Release ball at a wall as if shooting. BOTH sides."
med-ball-shot-simulation.mistakes: Using the arms only — the power must come from the hip rotation and weight transfer.',. Ball too heavy — above 3kg slows the pattern and trains grinding, not speed.',. No follow-through — the follow-through is where shot accuracy is trained.',. Skipping the backhand — most players are dramatically weaker on the backhand.',.
med-ball-shot-simulation.progression: Progress: Shuffle-step into shot simulation — adds one crossover step before the release.', | Regress: No-weight wrist rotation drill — practice the mechanical sequence before adding load.',

med-ball-slam.name: Med Ball Slam
med-ball-slam.execution: Stand with feet shoulder-width. Hold a slam ball overhead with both hands.',. Rise onto the toes — full body stretch at the top. Slam the ball into the ground as hard as possible — engage everything from the lats to the abs.',. Follow through — bend at the hips as the ball descends, don't let the back round at the bottom.',. Catch the bounce or pick the ball up. Reset and repeat.',. Every rep maximum power — this is not a conditioning drill at low intensity.',.
med-ball-slam.why: The med ball slam trains full-body downward power — the overhead-to-floor kinetic chain that develops the trunk flexion strength and explosive lat engagement used in physical play and body checking. It is one of the few exercises that trains the muscles above the hips in a true power expression, and it is completely safe to perform at maximum effort without a spotter. The slam also provides a psychological release that is surprisingly valuable in competitive athletes.
med-ball-slam.transfer: Trains explosive downward force — translates to checking aggression. Hockey check force = horizontal slam in shoulder pads. The pattern is identical. Train accordingly.
med-ball-slam.cues: "Reach overhead" · "Slam ball as hard as possible" · "Hinge to catch on bounce"
med-ball-slam.mistakes: Soft slams — these need to make a loud sound. Commit to every rep.',. Rounding the lower back aggressively at the bottom — hinge at the hips as you slam.',. Ball too light — 4-6kg slam balls give better feedback and more power demand.',. Too many reps per set (>8) — power decays. 5-8 reps per set maximum.',.
med-ball-slam.progression: Progress: Rotational med ball slam — slam to the side (like a slap shot backswing) for rotational power.', | Regress: Overhead press with the ball — build the overhead control before the slam speed.',

300-yard-shuttle-run.name: 300-Yard Shuttle Run
300-yard-shuttle-run.execution: Mark two cones 25 yards (23m) apart. Sprint to the far cone, touch the line, sprint back — that is one 50-yard shuttle. Repeat 6 times without rest (total 300 yards). Time the entire run. Elite hockey players target sub-55 seconds. Rest 5 minutes, then perform a second attempt. Average the two times for your official score.
300-yard-shuttle-run.why: The 300-yard shuttle (6 × 50 yards, or 25 yards × 12) is the gold-standard anaerobic capacity test used across the NHL, NFL, and NCAA combines. It maximally stresses the glycolytic system and demands repeated deceleration and re-acceleration — the same physical demand as repeated hard backchecks and forecheck cycles. A player who excels at the 300-yard shuttle will dominate the third period when conditioning becomes the deciding factor.
300-yard-shuttle-run.transfer: The classic hockey conditioning test — 25yd×6×2, training the whole energy system. Once a month max. The recovery cost is real. Treat it as a benchmark, not regular conditioning.
300-yard-shuttle-run.cues: "Out-and-back shuttles between two lines 25 yards apart. Max effort" · "No pacing. Track your finish time and beat it next attempt — same setup every retest."
300-yard-shuttle-run.mistakes: Going out too fast — pace yourself. The first two shuttles should feel controlled. Wide turns at the cones — sharp plants and cuts save critical seconds. Not touching the line — every cone requires a full stop and touch. Skipping the second attempt — the average of two tells you more than one.
300-yard-shuttle-run.progression: Progress: Improve your time by 1 second per month — a realistic and meaningful target. | Regress: 150-yard shuttle (3 × 50 yards) — half the distance, same mechanics, lower glycolytic demand.

battle-rope-intervals.name: Battle Rope Intervals
battle-rope-intervals.execution: Anchor the ropes to a sturdy point at floor level (post, tree, dedicated anchor). Grip one rope handle in each hand. Walk back until the ropes are taut. Athletic stance — feet shoulder-width, slight knee bend, hips loaded, torso braced. Drive alternating waves — one arm up, the other down, switching constantly. Power comes from the hips through the shoulders into the rope. Sustain wave amplitude (height) for the full 30 seconds. Waves should look identical at second 30 as at second 1. 30 seconds rest standing — let the heart rate settle slightly before the next round.
battle-rope-intervals.why: Battle ropes are the single most effective off-ice tool for upper-body conditioning, and a glaring gap in most hockey programs. Every other modality in the conditioning library trains the legs and cardiovascular system — none of them touch the shoulder, lat, and forearm endurance that hockey actually demands. A hockey shift involves constant upper-body engagement: holding a stick, fending off a checker, reaching for a puck, battling along the boards, winning a faceoff. The localized muscular endurance of the shoulders, traps, lats, and forearms is what separates a player who can sustain physical play for 60 minutes from one who fades. Battle ropes in a 30s on / 30s off format put those exact muscles under glycolytic load — the same energy system a real shift recruits. Programmed once a week, they restore the upper-body conditioning balance that lower-body-only programs leave incomplete.
battle-rope-intervals.transfer: Upper-body conditioning that translates directly to checking strength, stick battles, and board play. The sustained shoulder/forearm work mirrors the demand of holding off a checker while reaching for the puck — the only off-ice tool that builds this specific quality. Sustain WAVE AMPLITUDE the whole 30s. Dropping wave height = the set is over, regardless of round number.
battle-rope-intervals.cues: "Athletic stance" · "Slight knee bend" · "Ropes in each hand. Alternating waves — drive each wave from the hips through the shoulders into the rope. Sustain intensity for the full work bout. The 30s rest is to recover for the next round" · "Not to fully recover."
battle-rope-intervals.mistakes: Driving with only the shoulders — burns out fast and risks impingement. The hips and core power the waves. Wave height dropping mid-round — the rope flatlines. End the set; quality over time. Locked knees / stiff stance — robs the hips of their role. Stay athletic the whole round. Pacing yourself in early rounds — defeats the glycolytic stimulus. Every round is max-sustainable intensity.
battle-rope-intervals.progression: Progress: Heavier rope (50ft, 2-inch diameter) — adds load without changing format. Or double waves (both arms together) for a posterior-chain emphasis. | Regress: 20s on / 40s off — same intensity but more recovery between rounds. Build to 30/30 over 2-3 weeks.
battle-rope-intervals.muscles: Shoulders, Lats, Forearms, Core, Cardiovascular System

burpee.name: Burpee
burpee.execution: Stand with feet shoulder-width. Drop both hands to the floor just outside your feet. Jump both feet back simultaneously into a high plank position. Perform a full push-up — chest to floor, elbows at 45°. Jump feet back in toward your hands. Explode upward — full jump with arms overhead. Land softly and immediately begin the next rep.
burpee.why: The burpee trains the full-body metabolic demand of repeated explosive efforts — getting up off the ice after a hit, accelerating after a fall, or pushing through the third period when everything hurts. It combines a push-up (upper body), a squat thrust (hip flexors/core), and a vertical jump (power) into one continuous movement. Used correctly, it builds game-specific cardiovascular resilience.
burpee.transfer: Full-body conditioning with no equipment — builds game-ready fitness anywhere. If the push-up phase looks like a chest-flop, slow down and reset form. Bad burpees train bad mechanics.
burpee.cues: "Squat down" · "Jump feet back" · "Push-up" · "Jump feet in" · "Explosive jump at top"
burpee.mistakes: Sagging hips in the plank — maintain a rigid core throughout. Half-push-up (chest never touches) — go full depth or drop to knees. Barely leaving the ground on the jump — the jump must be maximal. Using burpees as pure conditioning at high reps with no quality control — form degrades and injury risk rises.
burpee.progression: Progress: Burpee broad jump (jump forward instead of vertical) — adds horizontal power demand. | Regress: Step-out burpee (step feet back instead of jumping) — reduces impact for beginners.

jump-rope-max-consecutive.name: Jump Rope — Max Consecutive
jump-rope-max-consecutive.execution: Standard rope length — handles at armpit height when you stand on the middle. Stand tall, elbows tucked, rope held loosely. Start jumping with both feet — small bounces, wrists do the spinning. Count consecutive jumps. When the rope catches your feet, stop. Write the number down. Goal: beat it next session. Progress: alternating-foot bounce, double-unders, criss-cross.
jump-rope-max-consecutive.why: Max-consecutive jump rope tests foot speed, rhythm, cardiovascular capacity, and coordination simultaneously — four qualities that map cleanly to skating. Sidney Crosby and Connor McDavid both train jump rope daily as part of off-ice prep specifically because of this multi-quality crossover. The score (consecutive jumps before missing) is a clean weekly benchmark: it goes up when foot speed improves, when cardio improves, and when CNS coordination improves — so it's a single number that tracks multiple adaptations.
jump-rope-max-consecutive.transfer: Foot speed + rhythm + cardio + coordination all in one. Sidney Crosby and Connor McDavid both train jump rope as off-ice prep. Beat your record every session. Progress to double-unders once 200 consecutive is easy. That's the elite benchmark.
jump-rope-max-consecutive.cues: "Count consecutive jumps without missing. Standard bounce" · "Light feet" · "Wrists do the work — not the arms. Stand tall. Eyes forward. When you miss" · "That's your score. Try to beat it. Progress: alternating feet" · "Double-unders."
jump-rope-max-consecutive.mistakes: Big arm swings — wrists do all the rope work; arms stay still. Jumping too high — small 1-2 inch bounces are all you need; high jumps slow the rhythm. Looking down at the rope — eyes forward, posture tall. Feel the rope, don't watch it. Wearing the wrong shoes — flat soles only. Running shoes with heel cushion kill the rhythm.
jump-rope-max-consecutive.progression: Progress: Double-unders — rope passes under feet twice per jump. The benchmark progression. | Regress: No rope, just shadow-jump the same rhythm — builds the bounce pattern without coordination demand.

jump-rope-hiit.name: Jump Rope HIIT
jump-rope-hiit.execution: Rope length: when you step on the centre, handles should reach your armpits. Start with double-unders or fast single-unders — maximum foot speed. Sprint the rope for 20-30 seconds at the highest speed you can maintain. Rest 30-45 seconds — walk or stand still. Repeat 8-12 rounds. Track your jumps per 30-second interval — compete against your best.
jump-rope-hiit.why: Jump rope HIIT (20-30 second all-out / 30 second rest) develops anaerobic capacity and foot-speed simultaneously — two of the most important athletic qualities in hockey. The constant low-level plyometric demand also trains the ankle and Achilles spring system. Elite boxers use jump rope HIIT as their primary conditioning tool because it mirrors the work-rest ratio and energy system demands of explosive sports — hockey included.
jump-rope-hiit.transfer: High-intensity intervals mirror the shift pattern of hockey — peak effort then rest. If you can't hold the same intensity by round 5, you went too hard on round 1. Pace it.
jump-rope-hiit.cues: "Max-pace skipping for the full 30 seconds — no breaks" · "No pacing. 30 seconds rest between rounds. Count your skips per round. If round 6 is way lower than round 1" · "You went out too hot."
jump-rope-hiit.mistakes: Too big arm circles — wrists drive the rope, not the shoulders. Jumping too high — 2-3cm off the ground is all you need. High jumps kill speed. Inconsistent work intervals — every sprint must be at maximum effort. Skipping rest — the rest period is part of the protocol, not laziness.
jump-rope-hiit.progression: Progress: Double-unders — rope passes twice under feet per jump. Elite conditioning and coordination demand. | Regress: 30s steady-state rope before attempting HIIT intervals.

mountain-climber.name: Mountain Climber
mountain-climber.execution: Start in a high plank — hands under shoulders, body in a straight line.',. Brace the core — the hips must not pike up or sag.',. Drive the right knee toward the right elbow, keeping the hips level.',. Return the right foot and drive the left knee toward the left elbow.',. Alternate at a controlled pace initially — increase to maximum speed as technique allows.',. The hips must stay level throughout — not bouncing side to side.',.
mountain-climber.why: The mountain climber builds hip flexor power, core stability, and cardiovascular conditioning simultaneously — making it the most efficient multi-purpose conditioning drill in hockey training. The alternating knee-drive pattern directly mirrors the hip flexion of skating stride recovery. Done at high speed, it raises the heart rate rapidly; done at controlled pace, it builds core anti-rotation strength.
mountain-climber.transfer: Combines core stability with conditioning — builds game-shape fitness. Pair with planks for full anti-extension + dynamic-stability work. Cheap, effective, no equipment.
mountain-climber.cues: "High plank position" · "Drive knees to chest alternately as fast as possible"
mountain-climber.mistakes: Hips piking up — this is a plank. Keep the body rigid.',. Slow, sloppy reps — either controlled for core work or fast for conditioning. Not in between.',. Feet landing too far forward — keep the knee drive below the hip.',. Holding the breath — breathe rhythmically with the leg drive.',.
mountain-climber.progression: Progress: Cross-body mountain climber (right knee to left elbow) — adds rotational core demand.', | Regress: Slow mountain climber (3s per knee drive) — builds the core stability before adding speed.',
mountain-climber.muscles: Core, Shoulders, Hip Flexors, Cardiovascular System

repeat-sprint-set-10-20m.name: Repeat Sprint Set (10×20m)
repeat-sprint-set-10-20m.execution: Mark a 20-30m sprint distance. Use a stopwatch. Sprint the distance at 95-100% effort. Rest 20-30 seconds — NOT full recovery. This is deliberate incomplete rest. Sprint again. Target: maintain within 5% of first sprint time. Repeat 6-10 times. If times drop more than 10% from the first sprint, the set is complete.
repeat-sprint-set-10-20m.why: Repeat sprint ability (RSA) — the capacity to sprint at near-maximum intensity repeatedly with short recovery — is arguably the most important physical quality in hockey. A player who can produce 95% of their best sprint speed on sprint number 10 is dramatically more valuable than one who fades to 75%. RSA is built specifically by practicing it: repeated short sprints with incomplete recovery.
repeat-sprint-set-10-20m.transfer: Develops speed endurance — ability to hit top speed repeatedly like a shift. Three sets max. Repeat sprint work taxes the CNS — recovery between sessions matters more than the work.
repeat-sprint-set-10-20m.cues: "20m sprint" · "40s rest between rounds. Maintain effort on EVERY round — if your time drops by more than 5%" · "The set is over. Quality > grinding through fatigue."
repeat-sprint-set-10-20m.mistakes: Going too easy on early sprints — you need to be near-maximal every rep. Rest too long — full recovery defeats the repeat-sprint adaptation. Not timing reps — without data you cannot know when to stop. Too many reps — 6-10 quality reps beats 15 sloppy ones.
repeat-sprint-set-10-20m.progression: Progress: Longer distances (40m) or shorter rest (15s) as RSA improves. | Regress: Longer rest (60s) initially to build sprint quality before reducing recovery.

shift-simulation-intervals.name: Shift Simulation Intervals
shift-simulation-intervals.execution: Choose a modality: bike, treadmill, rower, or court sprints. Sprint at 90-95% effort for 45 seconds — maximum sustainable intensity. Rest at easy pace for 90 seconds (1:2 work:rest ratio). Repeat 10-15 rounds — building to 18 rounds over the season. Track output on each interval — aim to maintain within 10% of first interval. Cool down 5-10 minutes.
shift-simulation-intervals.why: Shift simulation intervals replicate the exact work-rest ratio of a hockey game — 45-second all-out effort followed by 90 seconds to 2 minutes recovery, repeated 12-18 times. Training this specific ratio develops the metabolic fitness to maintain high-quality play in shift 15 as effectively as shift 1. No other conditioning protocol more directly transfers to game performance than game-specific interval training.
shift-simulation-intervals.transfer: Bodyweight shift simulator — 45 sec near-max effort + 90 sec rest mirrors the actual on-ice work:rest ratio. Twice weekly off-season, once weekly pre-season, zero in-season (you get conditioning from games). Cycle accordingly.
shift-simulation-intervals.cues: "45 sec mixed effort: broad jumps → burpees → run in place — go HARD the whole 45. 90 sec full rest between rounds. Simulates a real hockey shift: short max effort" · "Full recovery" · "Repeat."
shift-simulation-intervals.mistakes: Going too easy on the work intervals — 90-95% effort is mandatory. Rest too long — 90 seconds simulates the bench rest between shifts. Don't extend it. Not tracking output — performance monitoring is what makes this a training tool, not just fatigue. Starting with 18 rounds — build from 8-10 and progress over weeks.
shift-simulation-intervals.progression: Progress: Extend to 18 rounds or increase work interval to 60 seconds. | Regress: 1:3 work:rest (45s work, 2:15 rest) — more recovery for less-conditioned athletes.

skater-jump-intervals-hockey-tabata.name: Skater Jump Intervals (Hockey Tabata)
skater-jump-intervals-hockey-tabata.execution: Stand with feet hip-width on a non-slip surface. Athletic stance — slight knee bend, hips loaded. Push off the outside leg explosively, project laterally onto the opposite leg. Land soft on the bent leg, absorb the load through the hip and glute, immediately push back. Continuous bounds for the full 20 seconds — no pause between landings. Stay LOW the whole round. Drive HORIZONTAL distance, not vertical height. 10 seconds rest — stand still and breathe. Round 2 starts immediately after.
skater-jump-intervals-hockey-tabata.why: Skater jump intervals applied in a Tabata format (20s on / 10s off, 8 rounds) is the single most hockey-specific conditioning protocol that exists off the ice. Every other conditioning modality in the library is linear (sprints, bike, rope, row) or upper-body (battle ropes). Hockey is lateral — every stride pushes off an outside edge, every change of direction loads one leg, every check absorbed comes through the hip and glute on one side. Continuous lateral bounds under glycolytic load train the exact muscles (glutes, adductors, abductors, hip stabilizers) AND the exact energy system (lactic, ~75-90% VO2max) a real shift demands. Tabata's 20/10 work-rest ratio is the single most-studied high-intensity protocol in sports science — delivering gains in both anaerobic AND aerobic capacity in ~6 weeks. For hockey players, this protocol delivers what nothing else can: lateral-pattern conditioning at the intensity that translates to late-shift power preservation.
skater-jump-intervals-hockey-tabata.transfer: The single most hockey-specific conditioning protocol off the ice. Continuous lateral bounds in a Tabata format train the EXACT muscles and energy system of skating push-off under glycolytic load. Direct transfer to late-shift power preservation. If round 8 reps drop more than 25% from round 1, you went out too hot — pace and rebuild conditioning.
skater-jump-intervals-hockey-tabata.cues: "Continuous lateral bounds — push off the outside leg" · "Land soft on the opposite leg" · "Immediately push back. Don't pause between bounds. Stay low" · "Drive horizontal not vertical. The 10s rest is to stand and breathe" · "Not to fully recover."
skater-jump-intervals-hockey-tabata.mistakes: Standing up between bounds — kills the lactic stimulus. Stay low knee/hip flexion the entire round. Bouncing vertically instead of laterally — defeats the hockey carryover. Push wide, not up. Going out too hot on rounds 1-2 — round 8 should be within 25% of round 1. If it crashes, you paced wrong. Landing stiff on the inside leg — kills knees over time. Land soft, absorb through the glute, then push.
skater-jump-intervals-hockey-tabata.progression: Progress: Hold a light dumbbell in each hand (3-5 kg). Or extend to 30s on / 15s off rounds — moves it into pure lactic territory. | Regress: Lateral shuffle instead of bounds — same lateral pattern, less impact. Earn 5 clean Tabata rounds at the regression before progressing.
skater-jump-intervals-hockey-tabata.muscles: Glutes, Quads, Adductors, Calves, Cardiovascular System

slide-board-intervals.name: Slide Board Intervals
slide-board-intervals.execution: Set up the slide board on a flat surface. Booties over your shoes for the smooth surface to slide on. Stand at one end of the board, outside foot planted against the bumper. Push off the planted foot — long, deep stride — and glide all the way across the board. Plant the opposite foot against the far bumper, immediately push back. Stay LOW throughout. Continuous strides for the full 60 seconds — no pauses, long deep strides not short shuffles. 60 seconds rest standing or walking. Round 2 starts immediately after.
slide-board-intervals.why: The slide board is the single closest off-ice replication of skating that exists. Stride mechanics, energy system demand, even the specific muscle recruitment (glute med, adductor magnus, hip flexor concentric, posterior chain eccentric on the brake) — all mirror what skating actually demands. Programmed in 60s continuous rounds with 60s rest, the slide board delivers a 1:1 work-rest ratio matched to real hockey shift length (~45-60s). Glycolytic capacity in the EXACT muscles + the EXACT energy system a real shift recruits. Slide board intervals are the gold-standard hockey-specific conditioning modality in NHL strength programs — the carryover to on-ice performance is direct. For any player with access to a slide board, this is the closest you can get to skating without putting on skates.
slide-board-intervals.transfer: The single closest off-ice replication of skating energy demand. 60 seconds of continuous strides loads the EXACT muscles and the EXACT glycolytic system a real shift demands. Universal among elite hockey S&C coaches as the gold-standard hockey-specific conditioning modality. Universal among elite hockey S&C coaches for one reason: the carryover is direct. If you can do this clean for 5 rounds, your conditioning is hockey-ready.
slide-board-intervals.cues: "Push off the side bumper with the trailing foot" · "Glide across" · "Plant against the opposite bumper" · "Immediately push back. Long deep strides — not short shuffles. Stay LOW through the whole round. Quality of stride beats stride frequency."
slide-board-intervals.mistakes: Standing up between strides — defeats the position-specificity. Hips low, deep knee bend, sustained. Short shuffles instead of full strides — robs the carryover. Drive each push all the way across the board. Letting the inside foot drag — the planted foot fully releases, only the gliding foot is on the board. Pacing yourself — every round is max-sustainable. If round 5 is way slower than round 1, your conditioning is the limit.
slide-board-intervals.progression: Progress: Build to 6-8 rounds × 60s. Or add light wrist weights (1-2 kg) to load the upper body for a closer skating simulation. | Regress: Start with 30s on / 60s off, build to 60s on. Slide board is brutal on the adductors first time — back off if groin gets tight, build tolerance over 2-3 weeks.
slide-board-intervals.muscles: Glutes, Quads, Adductors, Hip Flexors, Cardiovascular System

ankle-alphabet.name: Ankle Alphabet
ankle-alphabet.execution: Sit on a chair or lie on your back. Lift one foot off the ground. Using only the ankle joint (not the whole leg), trace each letter of the alphabet in the air. Make the letters as large as possible — full range of motion. Go slowly and deliberately — feel the ankle working through each direction. Complete the full alphabet on one foot, then switch. If it's hard to trace distinct letters, reduce size and focus on control.
ankle-alphabet.why: Ankle mobility and proprioception are critical for edge control on skates — the ankle is the primary feedback mechanism between your body and the blade. Tracing the alphabet forces the ankle through its complete range in all planes, rebuilding neuromuscular control after sprains and maintaining the fine motor coordination that makes tight-turn edge work possible.
ankle-alphabet.transfer: Full ankle joint mobility and stability — comprehensive ankle prehab. Pair with calf stretching for full ankle coverage. Cheap, daily, takes 3 minutes.
ankle-alphabet.cues: "Seated" · "Foot in air" · "Write the alphabet with your big toe" · "Both directions"
ankle-alphabet.mistakes: Moving the entire leg instead of just the ankle — isolate the ankle joint. Going too fast — this is motor control work, not cardio. Only doing it when injured — best done daily as injury prevention. Stopping at 'Z' and thinking you're done — both sides, every time.
ankle-alphabet.progression: Progress: Single-leg balance on a foam pad while tracing — adds proprioceptive challenge. | Regress: Seated ankle circles (4 directions) before progressing to full alphabet.

fire-hydrant.name: Fire Hydrant
fire-hydrant.execution: Start on all fours — hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Spine neutral. Keeping the knee bent at 90°, lift the right leg OUT to the side — like a dog at a fire hydrant. Lift until the thigh is parallel to the floor. Do NOT rotate the pelvis. Hold at the top 2 seconds — squeeze the glute. Lower slowly (2-3 seconds). Complete all reps before switching sides. Add a mini-band above the knees for significantly more challenge.
fire-hydrant.why: The fire hydrant activates the gluteus medius and minimus through hip abduction and external rotation — the exact combination needed to stabilize the pelvis during single-leg skating strides. Weak hip abductors are directly linked to IT band syndrome, knee pain, and groin injuries in skaters. This exercise is a staple in every NHL prehab program for a reason.
fire-hydrant.transfer: Hip abductor strength that stabilizes the knee during skating push-off. Useful pre-skate or pre-lift. Five minutes of glute activation buys you 90 minutes of clean mechanics.
fire-hydrant.cues: "All fours" · "Lift knee out to side keeping 90° bend" · "Squeeze glute at top"
fire-hydrant.mistakes: Rotating the hip and pelvis to get more height — the pelvis must stay square. No pause at the top — the hold is where the glute fires hardest. Going through the motion without feeling the glute — if you don't feel it, slow down and focus. Only doing bodyweight — a mini-band makes this dramatically more effective.
fire-hydrant.progression: Progress: Fire hydrant with leg extension at the top — adds hip abductor and hip flexor endurance. | Regress: Side-lying hip abduction — same muscles without the all-fours balance component.

hip-flexor-activation.name: Hip Flexor Activation
hip-flexor-activation.execution: Lie on your back. One leg straight, the other bent at 90°. Lift the straight leg to 45° — hold for 3 seconds. Lower slowly. Switch. Or: standing, lift one knee as high as possible, hold for 2 seconds. Focus on the hip flexor pulling the thigh up — feel the contraction at the front of the hip. Progress to standing single-leg holds: lift knee, hold for 5-10 seconds, balance on the other leg. 10-15 reps each leg — deliberate and controlled.
hip-flexor-activation.why: Many hockey players have chronically inhibited hip flexors from prolonged sitting and skating — the muscle is tight but not strong. Activation work wakes up the neural connection to the hip flexors so they fire properly during sprinting and stride recovery. A hip flexor that activates slowly produces slower leg recovery between strides, which directly limits skating speed.
hip-flexor-activation.transfer: Ensures hip flexors are active before training — prevents hip flexor strains. Pair with kneeling hip flexor stretch. Stretch the chronically-tight side; activate the often-underused fibers.
hip-flexor-activation.cues: "Standing" · "Band at ankle" · "March knee to hip height slowly" · "Hold 2s at top"
hip-flexor-activation.mistakes: Using momentum to swing the leg up — lift controlled, feel the hip flexor fire. Only doing it lying down — transfer to standing and then to movement. Rushing — each hold should be deliberate. 2-3 seconds minimum. Confusing tightness for strength — a tight hip flexor often needs activation, not just more stretching.
hip-flexor-activation.progression: Progress: Standing hip flexor march with resistance band — adds external load to the activation. | Regress: Supine leg lift (knee bent) — easier starting position for severely inhibited hip flexors.
